executive_summary: The defining thread of today is the concentrated power struggle over artificial intelligence, its infrastructure, and its institutions — a contest that is reshaping technology, markets, and public trust simultaneously. The Musk v. Altman trial, now reduced to a raw credibility war between two men who each claim moral authority over the future of AGI, exposes how the governance of the most consequential technology in history has collapsed into personal ambition and narrative manipulation. Google's third-place standing at I/O 2026, despite its scientific AI dominance, underscores that the race is no longer about research prestige but about deployment power and coding capability — a competitive reality that is redrawing the map of who controls AI's near-term future. The Economist's examination of data center backlash adds a critical infrastructural dimension: the physical buildout required to sustain this AI arms race is generating genuine public resistance, making the question of AI's social license as urgent as its technical progress. Polymarket's insider trading signals, flagged by the New York Times, further illustrate that the financial machinery surrounding AI decisions is already being gamed by those closest to information flows. Taken together, today's content presents a single coherent alarm: the institutions, markets, and actors meant to steward AI's development are all under credibility stress at exactly the moment the technology is accelerating past our ability to govern it.

newsletters.title: 🔴 Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?

items.headline: Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?
items.blurb: A year ago I reported on the impact of artificial intelligence on the fight against climate change. On the one hand, data centres used a lot of electricity; on the other, that electricity was mostly renewable, and could be used to develop technologies that helped cut emissions around the world. Overall it felt like cause for cautious optimism, especially if—as we argued in an accompanying leader—AI companies would share more information about the impact of their systems to help consumers make informed decisions. A lot has changed since then. Some shifts were predictable. The amount of electricity the AI industry uses has exploded. The biggest models take more energy to train and run than they did last year, and they are being used by more people to do more things more of the time. Some adjustments were grimly inevitable. Where big tech companies once felt bound by promises they had made in a different political era to cut, or even reverse, their emissions, they now seem happy to switch on new gas turbines to power their growing ambitions. Other changes were more surprising. Last year data-centre impacts felt like a niche topic discussed by people interested in the overlap between AI and climate change. Now they are an increasingly important part of national—and international—politics. In America politicians are proposing regional and national moratoriums on construction, prompting entrepreneurs to wonder whether it might be cheaper to launch computers into space rather than fight through the morass on Earth.

longform.title: Musk v. Altman week 3: now the jury will pick a side
longform.thesis: The final week of the Musk v. Altman trial reduced to a credibility contest between two competing narratives: Altman as a self-dealing liar who betrayed OpenAI's nonprofit mission, and Musk as a power-seeking opportunist attempting to seize control of AGI.
longform.context: This newsletter dispatch covers week three of the ongoing Musk v. Altman courtroom trial, the culminating phase in which closing arguments and witness testimony forced the jury to adjudicate between the two tech leaders' competing characterizations of each other and of OpenAI's founding mission.
arguments: Altman's credibility was systematically attacked by Musk's legal team, with accusations of lying and self-dealing centered on OpenAI's contested transition away from nonprofit status — framing Altman as having betrayed the organization's founding principles for personal gain.

Musk was counter-portrayed by Altman's defense as a 'power-seeker trying to control artificial general intelligence' rather than a principled whistleblower, undermining his standing as a plaintiff motivated by mission rather than competitive self-interest.

The trial surfaced previously undisclosed internal details about OpenAI's governance and culture, including a 'golden trophy of a donkey's ass awarded to an employee who challenged Musk' — evidence used to illustrate Musk's retaliatory management style and contested authority within the organization.
longform.significance: The case forces a public legal reckoning over who controls the trajectory of AGI development and whether nonprofit structures can constrain commercially driven actors. The jury's verdict will set a precedent for how founding agreements and mission statements are legally enforceable in AI organizations. Coming amid simultaneous reporting on Trump's tech stock trades and Chinese AI advances, the trial sits at the intersection of AI governance, elite accountability, and the concentration of power in the AI industry.
questions_raised: Whether the jury will treat OpenAI's nonprofit founding documents as legally binding constraints on Altman's restructuring decisions, or as aspirational language without enforceable weight.

Whether Musk's simultaneous operation of xAI — which reportedly distills OpenAI's models — fatally undermines his claim to be acting in the public interest rather than as a direct commercial competitor.

longform.title: What to expect from Google this week
longform.thesis: Google enters I/O 2026 as a clear third-place foundation model competitor, with a critical coding deficit against Anthropic and OpenAI that its scientific AI dominance cannot fully offset.
longform.context: The piece previews Google's annual developer conference I/O 2026, written on the eve of the event by MIT Technology Review's Grace Huckins, who frames the conference against a backdrop of Google's eroded standing in the foundation model race over the past year.
arguments: Google has fallen to third place in the foundation model race primarily because of its weak coding tools: Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex are 'so dramatically superior' that DeepMind engineers were reportedly permitted to use Claude for their own work — a concrete institutional admission of competitive failure.

Google is mounting a coding comeback effort — a new AI coding team at DeepMind, involvement from Nobel laureate John Jumper, and a likely I/O announcement around the Antigravity agentic coding platform — but the author assesses this as insufficient to return Google to the coding frontier within the conference window, given how recently engineers were 'fighting over who got access to Claude Code.'

Science and health AI represent Google's genuine competitive strength: it is 'the only frontier AI company to have earned a Nobel Prize,' and tools like the AI co-scientist and AlphaEvolve demonstrate sustained leadership, though in health AI OpenAI's ChatGPT Health has seized narrative dominance while Google's forthcoming Health Coach appears narrowly scoped to fitness and diet advice rather than clinical concerns.

Organizational and political controversy shadows the conference: 600 employees, many from DeepMind, protested a DoD contract that Google signed the following day, and the author questions whether Google can 'maintain its veneer of neutrality' when such internal dissent is structurally unresolved.
longform.significance: The piece matters because it captures a precise moment of competitive repositioning in the AI industry — Google's transition from perceived co-leader to acknowledged laggard in the domain (coding) that currently defines model reputation. It also surfaces an underreported tension: Google's scientific AI work may be more consequential long-term than the coding benchmark wars that dominate press coverage, yet those advances receive systematically less attention.
questions_raised: Whether Google's strength in science AI can compensate strategically for its coding deficit, or whether coding capability has become the de facto criterion by which enterprise and developer adoption — and thus revenue and talent — are allocated.

Whether Google's Health Coach launch reflects 'appropriate caution in a high-stakes domain' or signals a second front on which the company has ceded initiative to competitors — a question the author poses directly but leaves unresolved.
